note_claims.claim: The patient presents with right-sided sciatica-type leg pain for 3 weeks.
The onset of pain occurred 3 weeks ago while lifting a resident at work.
Pain radiates from the buttock down the posterior thigh and lateral calf into the foot.
The patient reports leg pain is worse than back pain.
Pain is rated up to 7/10 and is worse after sitting.
The patient reports occasional tingling over the lateral foot.
There is no reported weakness.
There is no saddle anaesthesia or change in bladder or bowel function.
There are no reported fevers.
There is no history of cancer or unintentional weight loss.
The patient is taking over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily with little benefit.
The patient has no other medications and no known drug allergies.
The patient has no history of peptic ulcer, asthma, or renal disease.
Lumbar flexion is limited by pain.
Straight leg raise is positive on the left at 40 degrees and negative on the right.
Power, reflexes, and sensation are normal and symmetrical in both lower limbs.
The impression is right-sided sciatica, likely lumbar disc-related radiculopathy, with no red flags.
The plan is to stop ibuprofen and start naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food and omeprazole 20 mg once daily for 2 weeks.
The patient is referred to physiotherapy.
The patient is advised to keep active and avoid bed rest.
A fit note for two weeks is issued, allowing the patient to be fit for work with amended duties (no lifting or handling).
A follow-up appointment is scheduled in four weeks.
A symptom card is given to the patient.

transcript_facts.fact: Patient reports experiencing shooting pain going all the way down their leg.
The pain started about three weeks ago while lifting a resident at work.
Patient is a care assistant at a nursing home.
The patient initially stated the pain was in the left leg, but corrected themselves to the right leg.
The pain radiates from the bum, down the back of the thigh, round the outside of the calf, and into the foot.
The pain is rated seven on a bad day and is worse when sitting for a while.
The patient confirms the pain is definitely in the leg, not the back.
The patient reports a bit of tingling on the outside of their foot sometimes.
The patient reports no weakness, only pain.
Patient denies numbness around the bottom or between legs when sitting on the toilet.
Patient reports no change in waterworks (trouble passing urine or leaking).
Patient reports no problems with bowels or accidents.
Patient reports no fevers or feeling unwell.
Patient denies having ever had cancer or lost weight without trying.
Patient is taking Ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day, stating it barely touches the pain.
Patient reports no other medicines and no allergies.
Clinician asks the patient to bend forward and lift the right leg up straight to check for pain.
Patient reports pain shooting right down when the leg is lifted.
Clinician notes the pain is at about 40 degrees when the leg is lifted.
Clinician notes that the left leg is fine and power, reflexes, and sensation are normal and symmetrical in both lower limbs.
Clinician suggests the symptoms sound like sciatica, where a disc in the lower back is irritating a nerve going down the right leg.
Clinician plans to switch the patient from ibuprofen to naproxen 500 mg twice a day with food and add omeprazole 20 mg once a day for a couple of weeks.
Clinician plans to refer the patient to physiotherapy.
Clinician plans to give a fit note for two weeks, stating the patient may be fit for work with amended duties (no lifting or handling).
Clinician plans to review the patient in four weeks.

Clinician provides safety netting advice regarding cauda equina syndrome symptoms (numbness around bottom/genitals, difficulty passing urine, loss of control of bladder/bowels, or weakness in both legs).
